lead: Optimal control chooses the input u(t) that makes a total cost as small as possible, instead of merely making the system stable. For a linear plant and a quadratic cost J = ∫₀^∞ (xᵀQx + uᵀRu) dt, the best control is a state feedback u = −Kx. The gain K comes from solving the Riccati equation. LQR is used in drone flight, motor drives, satellite attitude control and process loops, where fast response must be balanced against actuator effort.
prereq: You need: state feedback and controllability from Unit 6, State Space Analysis, and the quadratic Lyapunov form from 7.5 Lyapunov stability.

blocks.text: An optimal control problem has a plant, a cost, and a class of allowed inputs. For LQR the plant is linear: ẋ = Ax + Bu. Here x is the state vector (n × 1), u is the control vector (m × 1), A is the state matrix (n × n), and B is the input matrix (n × m). The pair (A, B) must be controllable; otherwise no feedback can move every state.

blocks.where: J is the total cost. Q is n × n, symmetric and positive semidefinite (Q = Qᵀ ≥ 0). R is m × m, symmetric and positive definite (R = Rᵀ > 0). xᵀQx penalises state error and uᵀRu penalises control effort.

blocks.text: The cost is one number: squared state error plus squared control effort, integrated over all future time. The infinite horizon means the settled response matters more than a fixed final time. A drone holding position in wind shows the setting: quick correction is good, but violent motor commands waste battery and stress the frame. LQR turns a design argument into two matrices. Choose Q and R from acceptable deviation and acceptable effort, then compute the best feedback.

LQR is useful when a controller must respect actuator limits indirectly. A motor drive should reach speed fast without excessive current. A satellite should point accurately without burning too much fuel. The weights Q and R state that balance before any gain is calculated.
For the infinite-horizon problem, define P as the n × n symmetric positive semidefinite solution of the algebraic Riccati equation (ARE):

blocks.where: A, B, Q and R are the plant and weight matrices above. P is the cost-to-go matrix. For a scalar plant, P is one positive number.

blocks.text: Once P is known, the gain is K = R⁻¹BᵀP. K is m × n. The optimal control is u = −Kx. The minus sign is feedback: a positive state produces a negative input that pulls the state back.

items: Check (A, B) is controllable and the weights satisfy Q ≥ 0, R > 0.
Solve the ARE for the positive semidefinite P. Reject any other solution.
Form the closed loop ẋ = (A − BK)x and check its poles.
Simulate, then adjust Q and R if the response or the control effort is unacceptable.

blocks.text: The closed-loop matrix is A − BK. LQR guarantees that all its eigenvalues lie in the open left half plane when Q ≥ 0, R > 0 and (A, B) is controllable. This is the central result: the cost itself selects a stabilising feedback gain.

Q and R are not unique. Scaling both by the same positive number leaves K unchanged, because P scales by the same number and the factors cancel in R⁻¹BᵀP. Only the relative sizes matter. Increase a diagonal entry of Q to force that state to zero faster. Increase a diagonal entry of R to make that input smaller and smoother. Fast response usually costs larger control amplitude or a more oscillatory transient.

Q may have zero diagonal entries; it only needs to be positive semidefinite. R must be strictly positive, never zero, because free control makes the cost unbounded. Some syllabi call this LQ control or the quadratic regulator.

The proof assumes u can be any size. Real actuators saturate, so check the design against 7.1 Common nonlinearities. Model error changes A and B, so K may be suboptimal on the real plant. Integral action is added separately for constant disturbances. Output feedback needs an observer when only y is measured. Finite-horizon problems make P time-varying; this chapter stays with the infinite-horizon continuous case.

figure.caption: The weights Q and R feed the Riccati equation; its positive solution P fixes K, and u = −Kx closes the loop through the plant.

examples.question: For the plant ẋ = −x + u with cost J = ∫₀^∞ (x² + u²) dt, find the LQR gain K and the closed-loop pole. Use the infinite-horizon Riccati equation.
steps: Match with ẋ = Ax + Bu: A = −1, B = 1. Match with J = ∫(xᵀQx + uᵀRu)dt: Q = 1, R = 1.
Write the scalar ARE: AᵀP + PA − PBR⁻¹BᵀP + Q = 0.
Substitute: (−1)P + P(−1) − P(1)(1)⁻¹(1)P + 1 = 0. This gives −2P − P² + 1 = 0, or P² + 2P − 1 = 0.
Solve: P = [−2 ± √(2² + 4)]/2 = −1 ± √2. The positive solution is P = −1 + √2 ≈ 0.414. The negative value −1 − √2 ≈ −2.414 is rejected.
Closed loop: ẋ = −x + u = −x − 0.414x = −1.414x. The pole is −1.414, in the left half plane.
examples.answer: P ≈ 0.414, K ≈ 0.414, and the closed-loop pole is −1.414.
examples.check:
import math
p = -1 + math.sqrt(2)
k = p
pole = -1 - k
print(round(p, 3))
print(round(k, 3))
print(round(pole, 3))

traps: Choosing the negative root of the ARE. Reject P = −1 − √2 in the example; it gives K = −2.414 and closed-loop pole +1.414, which is unstable.
Setting R = 0. R must be positive definite; zero control cost leads to unbounded or impulsive solutions, not a normal LQR gain.
Using Q < 0 or an indefinite Q. Q must be symmetric positive semidefinite; a negative weight has no physical meaning.
Forgetting controllability. If (A, B) is not controllable, the ARE may not have a stabilising positive semidefinite solution.
Confusing LQR with pole placement. Pole placement picks poles first; LQR picks Q and R first, then the poles follow.

quiz.q: Write the infinite-horizon LQR cost and state the dimensions of Q and R.
quiz.a: J = ∫₀^∞(xᵀQx + uᵀRu)dt; Q is n × n and R is m × m for x ∈ Rⁿ and u ∈ Rᵐ.

quiz.q: Why does increasing R make the control smoother?
quiz.a: uᵀRu penalises control effort. A larger R raises the cost of input, so the optimum uses smaller u.

quiz.q: State the LQR stability guarantee and its conditions.
quiz.a: For Q ≥ 0, R > 0 and (A, B) controllable, the ARE has a positive semidefinite P, K = R⁻¹BᵀP, and A − BK has all eigenvalues in the open left half plane.

quiz.q: For ẋ = −2x + u, Q = 4, R = 1, find P, K and the closed-loop pole.
For the worked plant ẋ = −x + u, take Q = 1, R = 4. Find K and the closed-loop pole.
Why is the positive semidefinite solution of the Riccati equation chosen, not any root?
quiz.a: The positive solution gives the correct feedback sign and a stable closed loop. A negative P reverses the feedback and can destabilise the plant.

quiz.q: If Q and R are both multiplied by 10, does K change? Explain.
quiz.a: No. P scales by 10, so (10R)⁻¹Bᵀ(10P) = R⁻¹BᵀP. Only the relative sizes of Q and R affect K.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, LQR is often the inner loop of a larger design: a drone uses it for attitude, a car uses it for lane keeping, and a motor drive uses it for current control. Model predictive control extends the same cost to a finite horizon with input and state constraints, solved online. Linear quadratic Gaussian control adds a Kalman filter when the state is noisy. Search for algebraic Riccati equation, CARE, LQR weight tuning, and LQG.
